newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU chemical industry wants strong euro.
newsitem.headline: EU chemical industry wants strong euro.

text.p: Western Europe's chemical industry on Friday predicted faster output growth this year and next and threw its weight firmly behind the EU's planned monetary union, saying the euro should benefit competitiveness and growth.
The European Chemical Industry Council (CEFIC) said it welcomed the introduction of a strong single currency.
"The end of exchange rate fluctuations and distortions will allow companies to plan more reliably. The costs of foreign exchange management will be saved," said CEFIC president Jurgen Dormann.
Dormann, speaking at CEFIC's general assembly in Geneva, said that as a "sound international currency" the euro would improve investment conditions in Europe.

"CEFIC considers monetary union the necessary step to complete the full economic integration of Europe, it therefore welcomes the introduction of a single and strong currency," he said, according to a statement issued in Brussels.
Chemical companies were preparing for the conversion to the euro, he said.
CEFIC also said it hoped that as many countries as possible would be able to take part in economic and monetary union from the start.
"However, faced with a choice between accepting a lower number of participating countries at the very beginning, or a postponement, we would prefer the former," it said.
Turning to the near-term outlook, CEFIC predicted volume growth in the western European chemical industry at 2.5 percent both in 1997 and 1998, up from two percent in 1996.
Growth would be driven by an increase in exports of five percent this year, up from 3.9 percent in 1996. The forecast includes intra-European trade.
"Trends in the west European chemical industry magnified those observed in manufacturing industry as a whole, with the recovery taking shape in the second half of 1996."
However, even the more robust outlook for the industry would be insufficient to stabilise employment and further job restructuring was expected, albeit at a slower pace.
Inventories were thought to have reached normal levels, both within the chemical industry itself and with its customers.
"Exports are performing well due to the strong U.S. dollar and to sustained overseas demand, especially from the USA and South-East Asia," it said.

Low interest rates and solid profits were likely to stimulate investment, CEFIC said. "However, investment will be geared mostly towards expansion of existing operations rather than greenfield developments."
In terms of the individual sectors, plastics, organics, synthetic rubber and fibres are expected to be the most buoyant segments of the west European chemical industry this year.
"Growth in pharmaceuticals is expected to be more modest, largely as a result of government initiatives designed to check public spending."
